issues.description: The problem specification (and UML) defines checkOrderReady() as a parameterless method: +checkOrderReady(): void, and the textual description repeatedly refers to invoking checkOrderReady() without arguments. The solution implementation declares checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging), i.e., it requires a boolean parameter. This is a signature mismatch: students following the spec will implement a no-arg method, while the solution uses a different signature. This inconsistency can confuse students about the required API and how the method is intended to be used.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the solution's checkOrderReady method match the specification by removing the parameter: declare public void checkOrderReady() and adapt internal logging accordingly (e.g., always print required messages or use an internal flag). Alternatively, update the problem statement and UML to document the boolean parameter if that behavior is intentional.

issues.description: The problem statement (UML and requirements) requires a method checkOrderReady() with no parameters, but the solution implementation declares checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging). This changes the method signature of the same conceptual operation (checking and serving ready orders). Students following the problem will implement or expect a no-argument method; the extra boolean parameter in the solution creates a mapping mismatch and may confuse students when comparing their implementation to the reference solution or when using the intended API.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide the no-argument method expected by the specification. For example, add a public void checkOrderReady() { checkOrderReady(false); } wrapper (or remove the boolean parameter and control logging internally) so that the API matches the problem statement while preserving any debugging behavior.
